source.title_on_document: Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews

paper_design_summary: The authors build a maximum-likelihood estimator of the fraction (alpha) of sentences in a text corpus that were substantially modified or generated by an LLM, using adjective frequencies in known human-written reviews and in GPT-4-generated reviews. They validate it on pre-ChatGPT reviews mixed with AI reviews at known rates, then apply it to public peer reviews from ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023, EMNLP 2023, and Nature portfolio journals. They also compare alpha across subsets of reviews (near deadline, with citations, reply counts, reviewer confidence, and most convergent versus most divergent review of each paper in embedding space). No person was assigned to AI, and no creativity outcome is scored.

studies.label: Corpus analysis of AI-modified text in conference and journal peer reviews, pre- versus post-ChatGPT, with a homogenization comparison

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing. The paper estimates the share of AI-modified sentences in existing public review corpora and compares it across years and across subsets of reviews.
assignment.quote: The results, as shown in Figure 10, suggest that convergent reviews, which align more closely with the centroid of review embeddings, tend to have a higher estimated α.

arms.name: Pre-ChatGPT reviews
arms.description: Official reviews written before ChatGPT's release (ICLR 2018-2023, NeurIPS 2017-2022, CoRL 2021-2022, Nature portfolio 2019-2022); used for training and validation.

arms.name: Post-ChatGPT reviews
arms.description: Official reviews written after ChatGPT's release (ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023, EMNLP 2023, Nature portfolio 2022-2023); individual AI use is unobserved and estimated only at the corpus level.

participants.exclusions: No human participants are recruited. The units are public reviews (sentences within reviews). The number of distinct reviewers is not stated. Review counts: ICLR 2024 27,992; NeurIPS 2023 14,389; CoRL 2023 759; EMNLP 2023 6,419 (p. 6, Table 1); Nature portfolio 2022-2023 inference set 6,200 reviews of 2,189 papers (p. 42, Table 31).
participants.who: Peer reviewers for ML conferences (ICLR, NeurIPS, CoRL, EMNLP via OpenReview) and Nature portfolio journals; reviewers are not identified or counted.
participants.quote: We collect review data for all major ML conferences available on OpenReview, including ICLR, NeurIPS, CoRL, and EMNLP, as detailed in Table 1.
participants.locator: p. 6, Section 4.1 and Table 1; p. 42, Appendix G and Table 31

ai_tool.name_model: Reviewers' tools unobserved. The AI reference corpus was generated with GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613, June 13, 2023 snapshot); robustness with GPT-3.5, LLaMA-2 Chat (70B), Claude-2.1. Homogenization analysis uses OpenAI text embeddings.
ai_tool.how_used: Not observed. The paper infers corpus-level use; it reports that the estimates are consistent with reviewers using an LLM to substantially modify or expand their own review text (pp. 7-8, Section 4.6; p. 10).

task.description: Writing peer reviews of submitted scientific papers.

outcomes.name: Estimated AI-modified share (alpha) in the most convergent versus most divergent review of each paper (homogenization effect)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: For each paper, OpenAI text embeddings of all its reviews and their centroid; the review closest to the centroid is labeled convergent ('Homogeneous Reviews'), the farthest divergent ('Heterogeneous Reviews'). The MLE estimate of alpha (share of sentences substantially AI-modified, adjective vocabulary) is then computed on the convergent corpus and on the divergent corpus. Diversity defines the groups; alpha is the reported quantity, so this is an association between estimated AI use and similarity across reviewers of the same paper.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Most convergent review per paper (Homogeneous Reviews)
contrasts.control_arm: Most divergent review per paper (Heterogeneous Reviews)
contrasts.reported: alpha (CI ±), Heterogeneous vs Homogeneous: ICLR2024 7.2% (0.4%) vs 13.1% (0.4%); NeurIPS2023 6.1% (0.4%) vs 11.6% (0.5%); CoRL2023 5.1% (1.5%) vs 7.6% (1.4%); EMNLP2023 12.8% (0.8%) vs 19.6% (0.8%). Higher estimated AI share among convergent reviews, i.e., AI modification is associated with less diversity across reviewers (sign reversed relative to the codebook's diversity direction).
contrasts.locator: p. 35, Table 26; p. 9, Figure 10 and Section 4.7

diversity_detail.metric: Distance of each review's embedding to the centroid of embeddings of all reviews of the same paper; closest = convergent, farthest = divergent. The reported statistic is the estimated alpha in each group, not a similarity score.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: OpenAI text embeddings (model version not stated)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Within each paper, each review against the centroid of that paper's reviews; one convergent and one divergent review selected per paper.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: CI (±) on each alpha; Section 4.4 states 95% confidence intervals from 30,000 bootstrap samples for the main estimates; the method for Table 26 is not separately stated. No test of the difference is reported.
diversity_detail.notes: Observational association; the paper does not claim causality for the Section 4.7 correlates. Number of papers or reviews in each group not stated.

company_involvement.description: Second author Zachary Izzo lists the Machine Learning Department, NEC Labs America. No AI vendor is an author or funder; funding acknowledged from NSF, Chan-Zuckerberg Initiative, and Stanford HAI. OpenAI models (GPT-4, text embeddings) are used as tools.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author affiliations footnote; p. 11, Acknowledgments; p. 42, Appendix F

data_and_code.data_url: https://docs.openreview.net/reference/api-v2 (paper states all data are publicly available; reviews accessed via the OpenReview API /notes endpoint; Nature reviews scraped from journal pages)

eligibility.reason: Observational corpus study of public peer reviews; nobody was assigned to AI and individual AI use is not observed. Reviewer counts are not stated (tens of thousands of reviews). The main outcome is the estimated share of AI-modified text, which the codebook excludes when there is no diversity outcome. The paper does include one diversity-related analysis (Section 4.7, Table 26: convergent vs divergent reviews of the same paper in embedding space), so it may qualify as observational context; peer review writing is not a creative or ideation task in the codebook's sense, which makes even context status debatable.

one_line_finding: Estimated share of substantially AI-modified review sentences rose after ChatGPT to 10.6% at ICLR 2024 (from 1.6% in 2023), 9.1% at NeurIPS 2023, 6.5% at CoRL 2023, and 16.9% at EMNLP 2023, with no significant rise in Nature portfolio reviews (p. 21, Tables 7-8); reviews closest to their paper's review centroid had higher estimated AI share than the most divergent ones (e.g., ICLR 2024 13.1% vs 7.2%; p. 35, Table 26).
open_questions: Does a corpus study whose diversity analysis uses similarity as the grouping variable and estimated AI share as the outcome count as observational context with a diversity outcome, or should it go to the screening report as an AI-text-prevalence study?
Is peer-review writing within the creativity section's task scope (writing compared across writers for similarity), given the codebook's inclusion of such writing tasks under across_people?
notes: Outcomes not listed because they bear on none of the three questions: alpha by year (Tables 7-8, 12, 14, 16, 18, 30), by ICLR primary area (Table 10), deadline effect (Table 23), reference effect (Table 24), reply-count effect (Table 25), reviewer self-rated confidence (Table 27). Validation tables (Tables 5-6, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21-22, 28-29, 32-33) are semi-synthetic tests of the estimator. The Nature portfolio corpus was not part of the homogenization analysis (Table 26 covers ICLR2024, NeurIPS2023, CoRL2023, EMNLP2023 only).
